question: What does the “IP” in IP address stand for?
options: Internet Protocol
Internal Port
Identity Packet
Instant Pathway
explanation: An IP address is how Internet Protocol delivers packets to a host. Defenders note which addresses talk to their systems and treat unexpected ones as something to investigate, not as a toy to poke. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which addresses are reserved for private networks?
options: Only addresses that start with 8
Every address above 200
Only IPv6 localhost
explanation: Those RFC 1918 ranges are for inside a local network. They are not routed on the public internet, and they are not a security boundary. Anything that can reach the network can still reach those hosts, so segment and log. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is the main job of DNS?
options: Turn names into IP addresses
Encrypt every web page
Assign MAC addresses
Block phishing by default
explanation: DNS is the internet’s phone book. Attackers abuse it with lookalike names. Defenders log queries on resolvers they run, watch new domains, and read the real hostname instead of trusting link text. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which statement best contrasts TCP and UDP?
options: TCP checks delivery and order; UDP does not
UDP is always encrypted and TCP is not
TCP is only for email
They are two names for one protocol
explanation: TCP’s handshake and retries suit shells, the web, and mail. UDP suits lookups and live media where waiting is worse than a lost packet. Know which of your services should speak which, so a surprise protocol stands out. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What are the three steps of a normal TCP setup?
options: SYN, SYN-ACK, then ACK
GET, 200 OK, then FIN
ARP, DHCP, then ping
USER, PASS, then DATA
explanation: That three-way handshake opens a TCP session before application data. Lots of SYNs and few finished connections can mean a scan or a flood against a service you run. Log it and rate-limit at the edge. TLS has its own handshake later — don’t mix the two. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which port is the usual default for HTTPS?
explanation: Browsers expect HTTPS on 443. A “secure” prompt on a strange port is a reason to check the hostname and certificate. On a lab you own, don’t leave 443 open unless something should actually be serving the web. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which port is the usual default for SSH?
explanation: SSH on 22 is the standard encrypted remote shell. Telnet on 23 sends keystrokes in the clear — don’t use it. Prefer keys over passwords, avoid root login, and don’t expose SSH to the whole internet if a VPN or allow-list will do. Moving the port is not a real control. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What service usually uses port 53?
options: DNS
SMTP mail submission
MySQL
Remote Desktop
explanation: DNS uses port 53, often UDP for queries and TCP for large answers and zone transfers. Zone transfers should not be open to the world. On a lab resolver you own, very frequent or huge queries are worth a look. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why is RDP (port 3389) risky when published to the internet?
options: Attackers guess passwords against remote desktops
HTTPS stops working without it
It cannot be reached from outside
It patches Windows by itself
explanation: Remote Desktop is real admin access, which is why password guessing targets it. Keep it off the public internet. Reach it through a VPN, allow-list source addresses, require MFA where you can, and alert on failed logons. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is the defensive stance on port 445?
options: SMB file sharing — don’t expose it to the internet
Leave it open so certificates renew
It is secure DNS and belongs on every laptop
It is printer discovery with no risk
explanation: SMB lets systems share files. When it is reachable and unpatched it becomes a path for worms. Patch, disable SMBv1, firewall it so only the file servers that need it can talk, and never publish 445 on the WAN. You don’t need exploit steps to make that call. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What does HTTPS add that plain HTTP does not?
options: Encryption in transit and a certificate name check
Proof the website is honest
Automatic malware removal
A connection with no certificates
explanation: TLS protects bytes on the wire and lets the browser check the certificate’s name. It does not mean the site is trustworthy — phishing sites can have valid certificates. Read the hostname, not just the padlock. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is an HTTP security header?
options: A browser safety instruction sent by the server
The user’s password on every request
A firewall rule stored in the router
A malware signature
explanation: Headers such as Content-Security-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security tell the browser how to behave. They are free defense on sites you own. Test them in a lab before production. A missing header is a finding, not permission to attack someone else. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is Content-Security-Policy mainly for?
options: Limiting which sources may supply scripts and styles
Hiding the server’s IP address
Encrypting the database
Replacing passwords
explanation: A tight CSP makes many cross-site scripting bugs harder to abuse because the browser refuses unexpected script. Start in report-only mode on a site you own, read the reports, then enforce. CSP complements output encoding; it does not replace it. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What does Strict-Transport-Security ask the browser to do?
options: Use HTTPS for that host and skip plain HTTP
Disable JavaScript
Store the user’s password
Open the site in a popup
explanation: HSTS closes the gap where a first visit might still be HTTP. Only enable it on hosts you control that really speak HTTPS. Be careful with includeSubDomains — a mistake can stick until max-age runs out. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which control best reduces clickjacking?
options: CSP frame-ancestors, or the older X-Frame-Options
Turning off TLS
Using a shorter URL
Removing passwords from the page
explanation: Clickjacking hides your page in a frame so a person clicks your button thinking it is something else. frame-ancestors says which sites, if any, may embed you. Set it on apps you own, especially one-click sensitive actions. X-Frame-Options DENY or SAMEORIGIN is the older form. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why should every account have its own password?
options: One leak then can’t unlock your other accounts
So the password is easier to share
Short repeated passwords are safer
Browsers require identical passwords
explanation: Reused passwords turn one breach into many. A password manager can generate long unique ones. Turn on MFA for the manager and for email, because email can reset everything else. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is a password manager’s main defensive job?
options: Create and store long unique passwords for you
Share one master password in chat
Turn MFA off
Put passwords in source code
explanation: People are bad at uniqueness and length. A reputable manager, a strong master password, and MFA beat a clever pattern you repeat. Never put live passwords in code, tickets, or screenshots. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why prefer a long passphrase over a short tricky password?
options: Length multiplies the guesses an attacker needs
Symbols are illegal now
Short passwords make attackers quit
A passphrase cannot be hashed
explanation: Each extra character multiplies the search space. An original phrase beats a short word with a couple of symbol swaps. On systems you administer, set a real minimum length, reject known-breached passwords, and don’t force rotation unless you suspect a compromise. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What does multi-factor authentication add?
options: A second, different proof besides the password
A second copy of the same password
Automatic disk encryption
Immunity to every phish
explanation: MFA pairs something you know with something you have or are, so a stolen password is not enough. It is not magic: prompt fatigue is real. Prefer a security key where you can, and never approve a prompt you did not start. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: How is credential stuffing different from password spraying?
options: Stuffing replays breached pairs; spraying tries a few common ones
They are the same attack
Stuffing only works on paper mail
Spraying needs the site’s source code
explanation: Stuffing tries username and password pairs from old breaches. Spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts. Both show up as failures, then a success. On apps you own: rate-limit, require MFA, reject breached passwords, and alert. You don’t need to run either attack to detect them. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is phishing?
options: A fake trusted message meant to steal access or money
A brand of firewall
A legal port scan
Software that only runs on routers
explanation: Phishing shows up as email, text, or a fake page. Slow down: check the real sender domain, distrust urgency, and open the site from your own bookmark instead of the message’s link. Report the lure so the next person is warned. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is a safe first check before trusting a link?
options: Read the real hostname, not the visible label
Click first, then decide
Trust it if it uses your first name
Trust it if a padlock might appear
explanation: Link text can say your bank while the target is somewhere else. Preview the URL and compare the registered domain. Lookalike letters are a classic trick. When you are unsure, navigate there yourself. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: How is spear phishing different from a bulk phish?
options: It targets a specific person, often using real details
It only arrives on paper
It can never name a real company
It always uses a virus and never a link
explanation: Attackers read what you and your org publish, then write a lure that feels personal. “They knew the project name” is not proof. Verify unusual requests, especially payments, on a channel you already trust — not the contact info inside the suspicious message. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is pretexting?
options: A made-up role and story meant to break your process
Encrypting a disk without a key
Scanning for open ports
A header that blocks frames
explanation: “I’m from IT, read me the code” is pretexting. Real support will not ask you to skip the process you were trained on. You are allowed to refuse and call back on a number you looked up yourself. Praise the check; don’t shame the pause. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which pattern most strongly suggests business email compromise?
options: Urgent payment-detail change from an almost-right mailbox
An email that includes a company logo
A message sent during office hours
A newsletter you already subscribed to
explanation: Business email compromise is about moving money, not malware. Attackers spoof a thread or use a real compromised mailbox and change the destination account. Verify payment changes out of band, require a second approver, and still challenge “the CEO.” SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help against spoofing but not a stolen real mailbox. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is malware?
options: Software meant to harm, spy, or take control
Any program written in Python
A missed patch by itself
A long password
explanation: Malware is a purpose, not a language. It includes ransomware, stealers, and remote-control tools. Defense starts simply: don’t run untrusted attachments, keep backups the infected machine can’t rewrite, patch, and use normal endpoint protection on systems you own. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What’s the safest default for an unexpected attachment?
options: Don’t open it until the sender confirms out of band
Open it if the icon looks familiar
Enable macros so the document works
Forward it to the whole team first
explanation: Accounts get taken over, and display names are easy to fake. A document that demands macros is a common way to run code. If you must inspect a file, do it on a lab machine you can throw away, with macros still off. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is the practical defensive answer to ransomware?
options: Offline backups you have actually restored
Pay quickly so the price stays low
Unplug the monitor
Rename files so they can’t be encrypted
explanation: Ransomware encrypts or steals data and demands money. Payment is not a reliable way to get files back. Tested backups, least privilege so one user can’t encrypt every share, and no unnecessary remote access are the controls that hold. If it hits a system you own, isolate it and get a responder — don’t experiment on the only copy. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is a Trojan, in malware terms?
options: A program that looks useful but hides a malicious function
A routing protocol
A firewall brand
A form of strong encryption
explanation: The danger is invited in. Cracks and too-good free tools are common wrappers. Download software from the vendor you can verify, check signatures when they publish them, and treat a surprise installer on a lab box as something to wipe. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What does “living off the land” mean for a defender?
options: Intruders use built-in admin tools that look like IT work
Malware that only runs outdoors
An attack that always needs a brand-new bug
A law that bans security tools
explanation: Built-in shells and schedulers are not malware, so a file hash may never fire. Baseline who runs script hosts, from where, and when. Log process creation on systems you administer, and keep admin rights off everyday accounts so a stolen user password can’t reach those tools. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why log failed sign-in attempts?
options: They are often the first sign of guessing or stuffing
Successes cannot be stored
So you can collect passwords
Logs replace multi-factor authentication
explanation: A quiet account that suddenly fails dozens of times is telling you something. Log the time, account, source, and result — never the password. Alert when the count leaves its normal range. This is one of the first wires to add on a lab app you built. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: How is an alert different from a log?
options: A log is the record; an alert flags what a human should see
They are the same thing
Alerts are kept and logs are forbidden
A log exists only if an attacker sends it
explanation: Alert on everything and people stop reading. Log nothing and you cannot investigate. Pick a few high-value alerts — new admin, backup failure, a burst of sign-in failures — and keep broader logs for when you need to look back. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is appropriate to log on a web app you own?
options: Sign-ins and admin changes, but never the password
Every user’s password, in case they forget
Only successes, dropping every failure
Full card numbers, to make refunds easy
explanation: Good logs answer who did what, when, and from where. Secrets in logs become a second breach. Redact tokens, keep just enough of an id to investigate, protect the log store like production data, and choose a retention period on purpose. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why synchronize clocks on every lab system?
options: So events from different machines stay in true order
So passwords expire faster
So DNS is encrypted
Clocks don’t affect an investigation
explanation: A laptop a few minutes off can make “login, then alert, then block” look backwards. Point systems you own at a trusted time source and log in UTC. It is a boring control that makes every later control more useful. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is a false positive, and why does it matter?
options: A false alarm that trains people to ignore alerts
A confirmed intrusion
A backup that restored correctly
A password that was hashed
explanation: Detection is a tradeoff. A rule that matches too much gets muted. A rule that never matches gives false comfort. Tune on telemetry from systems you run: mark the noise, adjust, and write down why. Don’t “test” noisy rules by touching systems you don’t have permission to test. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: In a Linux lab you own, what does ls do?
options: Lists files and directories
Deletes the current directory
Starts a web server
Changes your password
explanation: ls is a read-only look around. ls -l adds owners and permissions, which is what you want on a lab box. Commands that delete or overwrite deserve a second look. Practice in a directory or VM you created, not on a system you cannot reinstall. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why shouldn’t everyday work happen as root?
options: A mistake or a bad program then owns the whole machine
Root is slower at reading files
Root cannot use the network
Only root accounts can be logged
explanation: Root bypasses ordinary file permissions. Use a normal account and elevate for the one command that needs it, so the elevation can be logged. The habit transfers from a lab VM you own straight to production. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: On a typical Linux system, what does mode 644 mean?
options: Owner can read and write; everyone else can only read
Everyone can read, write, and execute
Nobody can read the file
Only the group can write
explanation: The three digits are owner, group, and others. 6 is read+write, 4 is read. A world-writable file means any local account can change it. When you harden a lab service, secrets should be readable only by the account that needs them, often mode 600. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is sudo for?
options: Running one command with elevated rights, and logging who did it
Hiding a command from the logs
Turning file permissions off for good
Creating a wireless network
explanation: sudo is how you avoid living as root. Give a lab user the specific commands they need rather than blanket rights. Unexpected sudo is itself a signal. Keep the sudoers file under change control on machines you administer. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Why run a network service as its own unprivileged user?
options: A compromise then starts with that user’s rights, not root
So the service can read every private key
Unprivileged users cannot be monitored
Linux requires every service to be root
explanation: This is least privilege for daemons. A web server that can read the whole disk is one bug away from leaking it. Create a dedicated user, give it only the directories it needs, and drop root after binding a low port if you can. Practice on a lab VM you are allowed to break. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is input validation, from the defender’s side?
options: Checking data matches the shape you expected before trusting it
Letting the browser do all security checks
Encrypting the logo
A substitute for signing in
explanation: Validate on the server you control. Checks in the browser are for convenience and can be skipped. Constrain length, type, and allowed values. Validation is where a careful app starts; encoding and parameterized queries still matter beside it. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is cross-site scripting, conceptually?
options: Untrusted input runs as script in someone’s browser
A faster way to compress images
A lock that forces HTTPS
A database backup format
explanation: If a page you own echoes input into HTML without encoding, a visitor’s browser may run someone else’s script in that site’s session. Encode for the right context, use templates that escape by default, set a Content-Security-Policy, and mark cookies HttpOnly. Study this on a practice app you host yourself. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is SQL injection, and the standard fix?
options: Input changes a query. Keep it data with parameters
A way to speed queries by skipping passwords
A header that blocks frames
A kind of phishing email
explanation: If you build a query by gluing strings, a crafted value can change the sentence. Parameters keep the SQL structure fixed and the input boxed as a value. Use them everywhere you write queries, including labs. A low-privilege database account limits the blast radius. Don’t practice this on databases you don’t own. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is cross-site request forgery?
options: Another site sends a request using the victim’s cookies
A certificate that expired
Guessing a local password file
A DNS record type
explanation: The browser attaches cookies on its own. If a state-changing action has no secret the other site can’t see, that site can submit it for the user. On apps you build: SameSite cookies, plus a CSRF token for changes. Don’t accept state changes from a bare GET. Test the flow only on applications you own. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What does the browser same-origin policy do?
options: Stops a script on one origin from freely reading another
Encrypts the whole local network
Blocks every download
Replaces the need to sign in
explanation: An origin is scheme, host, and port. The policy is why a random page cannot read your webmail. CORS is how a server you control opts in to sharing. A wildcard CORS policy on an authenticated API is a mistake. Check it on a lab app you wrote before you ship it. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: How are authentication and authorization different?
options: Authn asks who you are; authz asks what you may do
They are synonyms
Authorization only happens on paper
Authentication is a kind of malware
explanation: A successful login is not a blank check. After you know who it is, every sensitive action should check a role or an owner. “Logged in, then change the id in the address and see someone else’s record” is a classic bug. Test those checks on apps you own, with two accounts you created. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give each person and program only the access the job needs
Give everyone admin so work never blocks
Use the shortest password the form allows
Turn logging off to reduce load
explanation: Extra privilege is extra blast radius. A lab notebook account does not need to be root, and a backup job does not need every secret. Review access on a schedule and remove what is unused. The same idea covers firewalls, file modes, cloud roles, and database accounts. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: Which line matches vulnerability, exploit, and patch?
options: Weakness, a way to use it, and the vendor’s fix
The patch is the attack and the vulnerability is the fix
An exploit is a firewall log format
All three words mean password
explanation: You can defend without writing an exploit. Inventory what you run, read what a weakness allows in plain language, and apply the vendor’s patch or mitigation. If there’s no patch yet, reduce exposure — take the service off the internet or add a control. Leave exploit development to people whose job and legal authority include it. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What is defense in depth?
options: Several independent controls, so one miss isn’t fatal
One long password and nothing else
Turning every machine off
A single allow-all rule with a serious name
explanation: MFA plus logging plus least privilege plus backups means a stolen password is not the end of the story. No layer is perfect. When you design a lab service, name at least two controls that would both have to fail before data leaves. Then check that each one actually works, on systems you may touch. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.

question: What has to be true before any security test?
options: You own the system, or you have clear written permission
It is on the internet, which counts as permission
You found a tutorial, which counts as permission
The port is open, so it is an invitation
explanation: Permission is the line between a lab and a crime. “Just looking” at someone else’s system can still be unauthorized. Get scope in writing: hosts, times, techniques that are off limits, and who to call if something breaks. Practice on your own VMs or student platforms built for it. Only test systems you own or have permission to test.
